idiom_name: default property values + value semantics: User() then mutate the copy
implementation_notes: Swift structs are value types whose properties can carry default values, so the valid instance is User() and the override step is a mutation of a fresh copy - var u = aUser(); u.email = "bad@example.com" - with no builder object and no risk that the mutation escapes, because assignment copies. The memberwise initializer also honours defaults, letting a caller name only the properties it passes, and a test-target factory (an extension or a static User.valid) keeps test-only defaults out of the domain type. Write a builder only for reference-type models (classes, Core Data objects, view objects) where a copy-with-modification idiom does not exist and mutation would alias the original.
code_sketch:
struct User {
    var name = "Ada Lovelace"
    var email = "ada@example.com"
    var age = 30
}

var u = User()                  // valid defaults
u.email = "bad@example.com"     // only the asserted field
XCTAssertFalse(canSendInvoice(u))
pitfalls: Value semantics stop at the first reference-type member: a class inside the struct is shared between copies, so cloning or replacing it explicitly is still the test's job.
Adding an explicit initializer to the struct removes the synthesized memberwise one, silently breaking the defaulted construction tests relied on.
Default property values live in production code; test-only defaults (fake identifiers, fixed dates) belong in the test target's factory.
